It's all about the angle of the wing. But I could be completely wrong, because that's only an impression I've gotten by looking at how airplanes and such changed over time at museums.

The wright brothers plane had flat wings with a curved top and did work on that principle, but I guess they sort of evolved that away as planes were developed more.
There is also a theory that it is because of the Coandă effect.

The notes you linked to are correct. Bernoulli's principal is often used as an interesting factoid when describing flight and lift. Unfortunately it's being misapplied here and doesn't provide the whole picture.

When describing lift people will mention the equal transit time of airflow over the top and bottom of the wing causing a significant difference in air pressure. This is incorrect, but not in the way you might think. In actuality, the airflow over the top of the wing will end up flowing faster than the air passing across the bottom of the wing. Here's a short article and video covering that. This still does not generate a high enough pressure differential to generate any significant amount of lift

What's really responsible for the lift created is a combination of the curvature of the wing and the angle of attack which displace air downward. This pushes the mass of air passing by the wing and generates a downward force. According to newton's third law a opposite upward force is generated which pushes the plane upward. The curvature of the wing assists by modifying the airflow so that it comes off the wing in a downward direction. This reduces the attack angle of the wing necessary to generate a given amount of lift. NASA Does a good job of covering this., and if you're curious, they also cover why other theories are wrong.

Bernouilli's principle is one of the reason why airplane can fly, but this is not the only reason. Depending on the wing's angle of attack, some effects are greater than others.

The main thing that is usually wrong when explaining how a plane can fly using Bernouilli's principle is the assumption of "Equal Transit" (two molecules near each other at the leading edge, one going above the wing and one going below the wing, will not end up next to each other at the trailing edge).

I personally think that Bernouilli's principle is put forward to make sure that pilots do not associate lift with angle of attack. When it comes to piloting a plane, the lift must be controlled by the engine power and must not be controlled by the wing's attitude (i.e. angle of attack). The latter controls only the plane's speed.

I'd say that a greater angle of attack does increase lift until excessive turbulence (stall) becomes too great. Also, the greater angles induce more drag. Source: used to play with wooden yardsticks on windy days as a kid.

A greater angle of attack does increase lift temporarily, but a greater angle of attack induces more drag as you mentioned therefore it decreases your speed too, which lowers the lift generated by the wing. This is an exercise that an instructor will have you do usually, i.e. when on a level flight you pull a bit on the yoke and keep it that way. The plane will climb a bit but then will slowly go down and go back to your original altitude. The main effect that pulling on the yoke has it to slow down the plane. Source: I'm a private pilot.

you pull a bit on the yoke and keep it that way.

Is it necessary to "keep it that way", or does returning it to the original position resume level flight? As in turning the steering wheel of a car and "keeping it that way" will result in a circle vs. returning it to center will result in a new direction.

Yes, it is necessary to keep it that way. If you let it go, you will go back to your original level flight/speed. Planes have an elevator trim if you need to keep your speed change for a longer time and relieve you from having to keep pulling/pushing on the yoke.
